podcast-joerogan-88KJ5rgCNmk:
Psychologist Jordan Peterson discusses women's studies with Rogan in an excerpt drawn from episode 877 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Peterson, then rising fast as a public critic of campus culture, states his case in the clipped, lecture-like style his fans know.

He argues that women's studies grew from ideology more than from open inquiry, and he questions what the field teaches about men and women. Rogan draws him out on how such programs shape students and policy. The excerpt preserves a key piece of Peterson's early public case, the academic fight that first made him famous beyond his classroom.
podcast-tuckercarlson-91PqJmEtFMk:
Margaret Roberts joins Tucker Carlson to present what she calls the true story of the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing, in which Timothy McVeigh's truck bomb killed 168 people at a federal building. Roberts argues the official account hides a wider plot and an ongoing cover-up, and she lays out the evidence as she has assembled it.

Carlson has revisited several settled cases on his program, and this episode follows that pattern: a researcher with a contrary file, given time to make the whole case. The mainstream record, built through trials and reporting, differs sharply from Roberts's version. The recording preserves her argument as she states it. Listeners can compare her claims against the court record, which remains the standard account of the deadliest act of domestic terrorism of its era.
podcast-tuckercarlson-lbDXrZdvXMk:
Economist and writer Glenn Loury speaks with Tucker Carlson about race, belief, and public life. Loury teaches at Brown University and has moved across the political spectrum. The episode title calls his account a confession.

Loury reflects on Gaza, campus speech, and losing a fellowship post. He recalls Malcolm X speeches and how they changed his views. The pair also discuss voter ID laws and claims of new Jim Crow rules. Listeners hear a personal story told by a scholar who often breaks with both left and right. His candor about his own past gives the talk extra weight.
